## Simulation for Lemma 3.2

In this simulation, we first randomly generate two groups of observation: $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ from the standard normal distribution, and the number of each group is given by $n_1$ and $n_2$. Based on our setting, we assume the latent aptitudes follow the Pareto distribution with $\alpha = 1.16$. Then we obtain the latent aptitudes for each group and check whether the paradox happens. We repeat this process 1000 times and record the frequency of the paradox occurs. 10 Monte Carlo iterations of our simulation are performed and we compute the average of the frequency. 

```{r cache=TRUE}
set.seed(13)

simu <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, size){
  simu_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k){
  
  Y1 <- sort(rnorm(n1))
  Y2 <- sort(rnorm(n2))
  
  order_pnorm <- function(q = 0, mean = 0, sd = 1, k = 1, n = 1e4){
    p <- pnorm(q, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
  }

  order_pnorm_vec <- function(q, mean = 0, sd = 1){
    q <- sort(q) 
    n <- length(q)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      order_pnorm(q[j], k = j, n = n, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    }))
  }
  
  u1 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y1)
  u2 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y2)
  
  order_Pareto_vec <- function(u, t = 1, alpha = 1.16, npop = 1e4){
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j]-n, n + 1 - j), t = t, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  # try it out on the percentiles obtained from order_norm_vec
  X1 <- order_Pareto_vec(u1, npop = N1)
  X2 <- order_Pareto_vec(u2, npop = N2)
  return(c(Y1[n1-n1j], Y2[n2-n2k], X1[n1-n1j], X2[n2-n2k]))
}
  res <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:size, function(xx){
    simu_paradox(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, N1 = N1, N2 = N2,n1j = n1j, n2k = n2k)
  }, mc.cores = 7)) 
  res <- as.data.frame(res)
  colnames(res) <- c('Y1', 'Y2', 'X1', 'X2')
  return(nrow(res[res$Y1 < res$Y2 & res$X1 > res$X2,]))
}

result_1 <- replicate(10, simu(n1 = 400, n2 = 600, N1 = 1e6, N2 = 1e6, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, size = 1000))
result_2 <- replicate(10, simu(n1 = 300, n2 = 700, N1 = 1e6, N2 = 1e6, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, size = 1000))
result_3 <- replicate(10, simu(n1 = 600, n2 = 400, N1 = 1e6, N2 = 1e6, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, size = 1000))
result_4 <- replicate(10, simu(n1 = 700, n2 = 300, N1 = 1e6, N2 = 1e6, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, size = 1000))

res <- data.frame(case = c('n_1 = 400, n_2 = 600, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6', 
                           'n_1 = 300, n_2 = 700, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6',
                           'n_1 = 600, n_2 = 400, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6',
                           'n_1 = 700, n_2 = 300, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6'), 
                  prob1 = c(0.1, 0.2, 0, 0), 
                  prob2 = c(mean(result_1)/1000, mean(result_2)/1000, 
                            mean(result_3)/1000, mean(result_4)/1000))
colnames(res) <- c('', 'Prob from Lemma 3.2', 'Prob from simulation')
knitr::kable(res)
```

## Simulation for Lemma 3.3

In this simulation, we first randomly generate two groups of observation: $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ from the standard normal distribution, and the number of each group is given by $n_1$ and $n_2$. Based on our setting, we assume the latent aptitudes follow the Pareto distribution with $\alpha = 1.16$. Then we obtain the latent aptitudes for each group and check whether the paradox happens. We repeat this process 1000 times and record the frequency of the paradox. 10 Monte Carlo iterations of our simulation are performed and we compute the average of the frequency. 

```{r cache=TRUE}
set.seed(13)

simu <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, size){
  simu_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k){
  
  Y1 <- sort(rnorm(n1))
  Y2 <- sort(rnorm(n2))
  
  order_pnorm <- function(q = 0, mean = 0, sd = 1, k = 1, n = 1e4){
    p <- pnorm(q, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
  }
  
  order_pnorm_vec <- function(q, mean = 0, sd = 1){
    q <- sort(q) 
    n <- length(q)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      order_pnorm(q[j], k = j, n = n, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    }))
  }
  
  u1 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y1)
  u2 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y2)
  
  order_Pareto_vec <- function(u, t = 1, alpha = 1.16, npop = 1e4){
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j, npop[j] - j + 1), t = t, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  # try it out on the percentiles obtained from order_norm_vec
  X1 <- order_Pareto_vec(u1, npop = N1)
  X2 <- order_Pareto_vec(u2, npop = N2)
  return(c(Y1[n1-n1j], Y2[n2-n2k], X1[n1-n1j], X2[n2-n2k]))
}
  res <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:size, function(xx){
    simu_paradox(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, N1 = N1, N2 = N2,n1j = n1j, n2k = n2k)
  }, mc.cores = 7)) 
  res <- as.data.frame(res)
  colnames(res) <- c('Y1', 'Y2', 'X1', 'X2')
  return(nrow(res[res$Y1 < res$Y2 & res$X1 > res$X2,]))
}

result_4 <- replicate(10, simu(n1 = 700, n2 = 300, N1 = 1e6, N2 = 1e6, n1j = 699, n2k = 299, size = 1000))

res <- data.frame(case = c('n_1 = 400, n_2 = 600, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6', 
                           'n_1 = 300, n_2 = 700, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6',
                           'n_1 = 600, n_2 = 400, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6',
                           'n_1 = 700, n_2 = 300, N_1 = 1e6, N_2 = 1e6'), 
                  prob1 = c(0, 0, 0.1, 0.2), 
                  prob2 = c(mean(result_1)/1000, mean(result_2)/1000, 
                            mean(result_3)/1000, mean(result_4)/1000))
colnames(res) <- c('', 'Prob from Lemma 3.3', 'Prob from simulation')
knitr::kable(res)
```


## Simulation for Lemma 3.7 in Uniform Distribution Example

In this simulation, we verify the uniform example with a Monte Carlo simulation. In each simulation, we first randomly generate two groups of observation: $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ from the standard uniform distribution, and the number of each group is given by $n_1$ and $n_2$. Based on our setting, we assume the latent aptitudes follow the Pareto distribution with $\alpha = 1.16$ and the $\delta = 0.001$. Then we obtain the latent aptitudes for each group and check whether the paradox happens. We repeat this process 1000 times and record the frequency of the Gould paradox happening. 100 Monte Carlo iterations of our simulation are performed and we calculate the average of the frequency divided by 1000 as the probability of the Gould paradox happening. 

```{r cache=TRUE}
set.seed(13)

simu <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, delta){
  simu_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, delta){
  
  Y1 <- sort(runif(n1, min = 0, max = 1))
  Y2 <- sort(runif(n2, min = 0, max = (1+delta)))
  
  order_punif <- function(q = 0, min = 0, max = 1, k = 1, n = 1e4){
    p <- q/(max - min)
    pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
  }
  
  order_punif_vec <- function(q, min = 0, max = 1){
    q <- sort(q) 
    n <- length(q)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      order_punif(q[j], k = j, n = n, min = min, max = max)
    }))
  }
  
  u1 <- order_punif_vec(Y1, min = 0, max = 1)
  u2 <- order_punif_vec(Y2, min = 0, max = (1+delta))
  
  order_Pareto_vec <- function(u, t = 1, alpha = 1.16, npop = 1e4){
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j]-n, n + 1 - j), t = t, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  # try it out on the percentiles obtained from order_norm_vec
  X1 <- order_Pareto_vec(u1, npop = N1)
  X2 <- order_Pareto_vec(u2, npop = N2)
  return(c(Y1[n1-n1j], Y2[n2-n2k], X1[n1-n1j], X2[n2-n2k]))
}
  res <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:1000, function(xx){
    simu_paradox(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, N1 = N1, N2 = N2, n1j = n1j, n2k = n2k, delta = delta)
  }, mc.cores = 7)) 
  res <- as.data.frame(res)
  colnames(res) <- c('Y1', 'Y2', 'X1', 'X2')
  return(nrow(res[res$Y1 < res$Y2 & res$X1 > res$X2,]))
}

result_1 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 40, n2 = 60, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 1e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, delta = 0.001))
result_2 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 30, n2 = 70, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 1e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, delta = 0.001))
result_3 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 60, n2 = 40, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 1e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, delta = 0.001))
result_4 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 70, n2 = 30, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 1e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, delta = 0.001))

num_1 <- round(60/(40+60)*(1+0.001)^40 - 1e5/(1e5+1e5), 4)
num_2 <- round(70/(30+70)*(1+0.001)^30 - 1e5/(1e5+1e5), 4)
num_3 <- round(40/(60+40)*(1+0.001)^60 - 1e5/(1e5+1e5), 4)
num_4 <- round(30/(70+30)*(1+0.001)^70 - 1e5/(1e5+1e5), 4)
res <- data.frame(case = c('n_1 = 40, n_2 = 60, N_1 = 1e5, N_2 = 1e5', 
                           'n_1 = 30, n_2 = 70, N_1 = 1e5, N_2 = 1e5',
                           'n_1 = 60, n_2 = 40, N_1 = 1e5, N_2 = 1e5',
                           'n_1 = 70, n_2 = 30, N_1 = 1e5, N_2 = 1e5'), 
                  prob1 = c(round(ifelse(num_1 > 0, num_1, 0), 4), 
                            round(ifelse(num_2 > 0, num_2, 0), 4), 
                            round(ifelse(num_3 > 0, num_3, 0), 4), 
                            round(ifelse(num_4 > 0, num_4, 0), 4)), 
                  prob2 = c(mean(result_1)/1000, mean(result_2)/1000, 
                            mean(result_3)/1000, mean(result_4)/1000))
colnames(res) <- c('', 'Prob from Lemma 3.7 in Uniform', 'Prob from simulation')
knitr::kable(res)
```

## Simulation for Lemma 3.7 in Normal Distribution Example

In this simulation, we verify the normal example with a Monte Carlo simulation. In each simulation, we first randomly generate two groups of observation: $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ from the normal distribution with $\mu_1 = -1$ and $\mu_2 = 1$, and the number of each group is given by $n_1$ and $n_2$. Based on our setting, we assume the latent aptitudes follow the Pareto distribution with $\alpha = 1.16$, $N_1 = 1e5$ and $N_2 = 2e5$. Then we obtain the latent aptitudes for each group and check whether the paradox happens. We repeat this process 1000 times and record the frequency of the Gould paradox happening. 1000 Monte Carlo iterations of our simulation are performed and we calculate the average of the frequency divided by 1000 as the probability of the Gould paradox happening. Next, using the procedure in \cite{mi2009mvtnorm}, we calculate the probability of our outcome, which involves the probability of a multivariate normal distribution. 


```{r cache=TRUE}
set.seed(13)

simu <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  simu_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  
  Y1 <- sort(rnorm(n1, mu1, sigma1))
  Y2 <- sort(rnorm(n2, mu2, sigma2))
  
  order_pnorm <- function(q = 0, mean = 0, sd = 1, k = 1, n = 1e4){
    p <- pnorm(q, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
  }
  
  order_pnorm_vec <- function(q, mean = 0, sd = 1){
    q <- sort(q) 
    n <- length(q)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      order_pnorm(q[j], k = j, n = n, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    }))
  }
  
  u1 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y1, mean = mu1, sd = sigma1)
  u2 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y2, mean = mu2, sd = sigma2)
  
  order_Pareto_vec <- function(u, t = 1, alpha = 1.16, npop = 1e4){
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j]-n, n + 1 - j), t = t, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  # try it out on the percentiles obtained from order_norm_vec
  X1 <- order_Pareto_vec(u1, npop = N1)
  X2 <- order_Pareto_vec(u2, npop = N2)
  return(c(Y1[n1-n1j], Y2[n2-n2k], X1[n1-n1j], X2[n2-n2k]))
}

  res <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:1000, function(xx){
    simu_paradox(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, N1 = N1, N2 = N2, n1j = n1j, n2k = n2k, 
                 mu1 = mu1, mu2 = mu2, sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)
  }, mc.cores = 7)) 
  res <- as.data.frame(res)
  colnames(res) <- c('Y1', 'Y2', 'X1', 'X2')
  return(nrow(res[res$Y1 < res$Y2 & res$X1 > res$X2,]))
}

result_1 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 40, n2 = 60, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 2, sigma2 = 4))
result_2 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 30, n2 = 70, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 2, sigma2 = 4))

                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 2, sigma2 = 4))
result_4 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 100, n2 = 10, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 2, sigma2 = 4))
result_5 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 40, n2 = 60, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 1, sigma2 = 1))
result_6 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 30, n2 = 70, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 1, sigma2 = 1))
result_7 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 10, n2 = 100, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 1, sigma2 = 1))
result_8 <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = 100, n2 = 10, N1 = 1e5, N2 = 2e5, n1j = 0, n2k = 0, 
                                mu1 = -1, mu2 = 1, sigma1 = 1, sigma2 = 1))

prob_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  x <- c(rep((mu2-mu1)/sigma1, n1), rep(0, (n2-1)))
  mu <- rep(0, (n1+n2-1))
  sigma <- diag((n1+n2-1))
  sigma[1:n1, 1:n1] <- sigma[1:n1, 1:n1] + (sigma2^2/sigma1^2)
  sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), 1:n1] <- 
    sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), 1:n1] + (sigma2/sigma1)
  sigma[1:n1, (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] <- 
    sigma[1:n1, (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] + (sigma2/sigma1)
  sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] <- 
    sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] + 1
  
  return(n2*pmvnorm(lower = -Inf, upper = x, mean = mu, sigma = sigma) - 
           (N2/(N1+N2)))
}
```

## Simulation for Educational Attainment Example

In this simulation, we simulate the process of students moving on to the next level of education from primary school to the university. First, we randomly generate 1 million talents from Pareto distribution, which corresponds to the 1 million talents of primary school students. Then we randomly generate 2 thousand school indices from 1 to 2000 and assign them to the students we generate before, which represent the schools that the students will attend. Finally, we transform ordered talents corresponding to the eligible population to percentiles from the ordered statistics and convert percentiles to ordered scores from a normal distribution, which could represent the scores the students achieve in the schools.  

The final step can be described in the following formula: 

\begin{equation} \label{eq:estiY}
	Y_{i,(j)} = F_{Y_{i}}^{-1} \left( F_{X_{i}}\left(X_{i, (500*(i-1) + j))} \right) \right)
\end{equation}

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{X_i}\left(X_{i,(j)} \right) & \sim U_{i,(j)}, 
F_{X_{i,(j)}}\left(X_{i,(j)} \right) & \sim U_{i,j}
\end{aligned}
$$
where 
$\sim$ means distributed as, $U_{i,j} \sim U(0,1)$, and $U_{i,(j)} \sim \operatorname{Beta}(j, n_i+1-j)$. 


$X_{i, (j)}$ is the jth ordered talent in the ith school. $F_{X_{i}}$ is the cumulative distribution function of talents in the ith school. $Y_{i, (j)}$ is the jth ordered score in the ith school. $F_{Y_{i}}$ is the cumulative distribution function of scores in the ith school. 

The score distribution for each school follows the Normal distribution with different parameters. We assume the mean of the Normal distribution ranges from 60 to 80, which indicates the different levels of schools. Better schools have higher mean scores. The standard deviation for the first figure is 2 and the second is 5. 

50 Monte Carlo iterations of our simulation are performed. The tendencies of the most talented students in each of the 50 simulations are displayed in the following figures. The primary\_index0 in the x-axis indicates the initial schools for the students with the highest talent. The levels of schools are represented by the index on the y-axis, which goes from 1 to 2000. High-achieving schools are a sign of superiority. The following are the schools that students will attend: primary\_index1 through primary\_index3. It is evident that even if gifted children begin their education at a lesser school, they may advance to a top institution within two to three stages. 

```{r cache=TRUE, cache.lazy = FALSE}
set.seed(13)
simu_primary <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:50, mc.cores = 7, FUN = function(xx){
  
  ## 1 million students eligible for school
  
  ## 2e3 primary school
  talent_index = data.frame(talent = rPareto(n = 1e6, t = 1, alpha = 1.16), 
                      primary_index0 = rep(c(1:2e3), 500)) %>% 
    arrange(talent)
  
  ## average scores range from 60 to 80
  ## no information on sd
  primary_mean <- seq(60, 80, length.out = 2e3)
  primary_sd <- 2
  
  ## percentiles are order statistics from Pareto distribution
  u = unlist(lapply(1:1e6, function(j){
    pbeta(pPareto(talent_index$talent[j], t = 1, alpha = 1.16), j, 1e6-j+1)
  }))
  
  ## map the percentiles to different primary schools
  m <- sapply(1:2e3, function(x){
    #n <- length(order_talent[[x]])
    n <- 500
    qnorm(qbeta(u[talent_index$primary_index0 == x], 
                shape1 = 1:n, shape2 = n:1), 
          mean = primary_mean[x], sd = primary_sd)
  })
  
  score1 <- c()
  for (i in 1:2e3) {
    score1[talent_index$primary_index0 == i] <- m[,i]
  }
  all_talent <- talent_index %>% 
    mutate(u = u, score1 = score1) %>% 
    arrange(score1) %>% 
    mutate(primary_index1 = sort(rep(c(1:2e3), 500))) %>% 
    arrange(talent)
  
  ## map the percentiles to different primary schools
  m <- sapply(1:2e3, function(x){
    #n <- length(order_talent[[x]])
    n <- 500
    qnorm(qbeta(u[all_talent$primary_index1 == x], 
                shape1 = 1:n, shape2 = n:1), 
          mean = primary_mean[x], sd = primary_sd)
  })
  
  score2 <- c()
  for (i in 1:2e3) {
    score2[all_talent$primary_index1 == i] <- m[,i]
  }
  
  all_talent <- all_talent %>% 
    mutate(u = u, score2 = score2) %>% 
    arrange(score2) %>% 
    mutate(primary_index2 = sort(rep(c(1:2e3), 500))) %>% 
    arrange(talent)
  
  
  ## map the percentiles to different primary schools
  m <- sapply(1:2e3, function(x){
    #n <- length(order_talent[[x]])
    n <- 500
    qnorm(qbeta(u[all_talent$primary_index2 == x], 
                shape1 = 1:n, shape2 = n:1), 
          mean = primary_mean[x], sd = primary_sd)
  })
  
  score3 <- c()
  for (i in 1:2e3) {
    score3[all_talent$primary_index2 == i] <- m[,i]
  }
  
  all_talent <- all_talent %>% 
    mutate(u = u, score3 = score3) %>% 
    arrange(score3) %>% 
    mutate(primary_index3 = sort(rep(c(1:2e3), 500))) %>% 
    arrange(talent)
  
  cbind(simu = xx, all_talent)
}))

t <- simu_primary %>% group_by(simu) %>% top_n(1, talent)

talent_max <- pivot_longer(
  data = t,
  cols = starts_with("primary"),
  names_to = "round",
  values_to = "index"
)

ggplot(talent_max, aes(x = round, y = index, group = simu)) +
  geom_line(aes(color=simu))+
  geom_point(aes(color=simu))
```

## Simulation for Major League Baseball Example 1

In this simulation, we estimate the performance of those who played in the league during WWII (World War II) if WWII hadn't occurred and the players served in the war would still be playing. For example, we are interested in the bWAR (baseball-reference Win Above Replacement) of Dizzy Trout if the Bob Feller were playing in the 1944 season. In fact, Bob Feller served in the Army during the WWII and he was a superior pitcher compared to Dizzy Trout. 

We displays the performance of Spud Chandler, Dizzy Trout, and Hal Newhouser when the top talented players served in the Army or not. We assume only two pitchers would outperform Spud Chandler in the 1943 season, Dizzy Trout in the 1944 season, and Hal Newhouser in the 1945 season. Additionally, we exclude the WWII correction for the MLB-eligible population when the top talented players did not serve in the Army.

```{r cache=TRUE}
ncores <- detectCores() - 1
years <- 1871:2023

## Assumed top two pitchers got removed
talent_computing_nonpara_3rd <- function(dataset, component_name, year, ystar, alpha){
  
  Ftilde <- function(y, t, ystar, component_name){
    y <- sort(y)
    n <- length(y)
    ytilde <- rep(0, n + 1)
    
    if (component_name == 'bWAR' | component_name == 'fWAR' | component_name == 'ERA') {
      ytilde[1] <- y[1] - (y[2] - y[1])
    }
    if (component_name == 'HR'| component_name == 'BB') {
      # since the minimal HR is greater or equal to 0.
      ytilde[1] <- 0
    }
    if (component_name == 'bWAR_p' | component_name == 'fWAR_p') {
      ytilde[1] <- y[1] - (y[2] - y[1])/10
    }
    if (component_name == 'SO' | component_name == 'AVG') {
      ytilde[1] <- ifelse(y[1] - (y[2] - y[1]) < 0, 0, y[1] - (y[2] - y[1]) )
    }
    
    ytilde[n+1] <- y[n] + ystar
    ytilde[2:n] <- unlist(lapply(2:n, function(j){
      (y[j]+y[j-1])/2
    }))
    
    if (t >= ytilde[n+1]) {
      1 - 0.1^7
    } else if (t <= ytilde[1]) {
      0
    } else {
      j <- length(which(ytilde < t))
      (j - 1) / n + (t - ytilde[j]) / (n*(ytilde[j+1] - ytilde[j]))
    }
    
  }
  
  Aptitude_nonpara <- function(p, alpha, npop){
    
    # converts order stats to their percentiles
    order_pbino <- function(p = 0, k = 1, n = 1e4){
      pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
    }
    
    # converts a vector of order stats 
    # to their percentiles. This vector should be the entire 
    # sample sorted in increasing order
    p <- sort(p) # just in case
    n <- length(p)
    u = unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      #order_pbino(p[j], k = 251-n+j, n = 251)
      order_pbino(p[j], k = j, n = n)
    }))
    
    # transforms percentiles from order stats (in increasing order)
    # to Pareto values corresponding to the general population 
    # of a greater than or equal to size
    # default alpha is that of the Pareto principle 80-20
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j] -n -2 , n + 1 - j +2), t = 1, alpha = alpha)
      #qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j] -n + 251-n , n + 1 - j), t = 1, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  foo <- dataset %>% filter(yearID == year) %>% 
    arrange(comp) 
  bar <- foo %>% filter(full_time == 'Y')
  full_comp <- bar$comp
  ## batter WAR talent
  bar <- bar %>% 
    mutate(WAR_talent = 
             Aptitude_nonpara(p = unlist(lapply(comp, function(xx) 
               Ftilde(y = comp, t = xx, ystar = ystar, component_name = component_name))), alpha = alpha, npop = pops))
  
  max_WAR_talent <- max(bar$WAR_talent) - 1
  range <- which(!(foo$playerID %in% bar$playerID))
  
  ## using the distribution from full time players
  bar <- rbind(bar, do.call(rbind, lapply(range, function(j){
    rbind(bar %>% dplyr::select(-WAR_talent), foo[j, ]) %>% arrange(comp) %>%
      mutate(WAR_talent = Aptitude_nonpara(p = unlist(lapply(comp, function(xx) 
        Ftilde(y = full_comp, t = xx, ystar = ystar, component_name = component_name))), alpha = alpha, npop = pops)) %>%
      filter(full_time == 'N') %>% 
      mutate(WAR_talent = ifelse(WAR_talent > max_WAR_talent+1, max_WAR_talent, WAR_talent))
  })))
  bar %>% mutate(ystar = ystar)
}

## Load MLB eligible population without WWII correction

rotation_bound <- as.data.frame(cbind(years, unlist(mclapply(years, mc.cores = ncores, function(yr){
  foo <- getRetrosheet(type = "game", year = yr)
  Tms <- unique(foo$HmTm)
  
  starter <- lapply(Tms, function(tm){
    bar <- foo %>% filter(VisTm == tm | HmTm == tm) %>% 
      select(VisTm, HmTm, VisStPchID, HmStPchID, VisTmGNum, HmTmGNum)
    t(apply(bar, 1, function(xx){
      y <- NULL
      if(xx[2] == tm){
        y <- xx[4]
      }
      else{
        y <- xx[3]
      }
    })) 
  })
  
  y <- unlist(lapply(starter, function(xx){
    unlist(lapply(1:length(xx), function(j){
      flag <- TRUE
      k <- 1
      if(j > 1){
        while(flag){
          flag <- length(xx[(j-k):j]) == length(unique(xx[(j-k):j]))
          if(!flag){
            break
          }
          else{
            k <- k + 1
          }
          if(k == j){
            break
          }
        }
      }
      k
    }))
  }))
  mean(y)
  
}))))

  int
}, mc.cores = ncores)) 

career_kAB_hal <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:nrow(pitchers_talent_hal), function(xx){
  int <- career_talent_nonpara(dataset = pitchers_talent_bWAR, component_name = 'bWAR_p', 
                               snippet = pitchers_talent_hal[xx,], alpha = 1.16)
  int
}, mc.cores = ncores)) 

mapped_quan_p <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(years, function(xx){
  pitchers_full <- pitchers %>% filter(yearID == xx) %>% 
    filter(full_time == 'Y') %>% arrange(-IP)
  pitchers_less <- pitchers %>% filter(yearID == xx) %>% 
    filter(full_time == 'N') %>% arrange(-IP)
  
  n1 <- nrow(pitchers_full)
  n2 <- nrow(pitchers_less)
  
  mapped_IP_full <- c()
  mapped_IP_less <- c()
  for (yy in c(1977:1980, 1982:1989)) {
    pitchers_ref_full <- pitchers %>% 
      filter(yearID == yy, full_time == 'Y') %>% arrange(-IP)
    pitchers_ref_less <- pitchers %>% 
      filter(yearID == yy, full_time == 'N') %>% arrange(-IP)
    n1r <- nrow(pitchers_ref_full)
    n2r <- nrow(pitchers_ref_less)
    
    mapped_IP_full <- cbind(mapped_IP_full, approx(x = seq((n1r-1),0)/(n1r-1), 
                                                   y = pitchers_ref_full$IP,
                                                   xout = seq((n1-1),0)/(n1-1))$y)
    mapped_IP_less <- cbind(mapped_IP_less, approx(x = seq((n2r-1),0)/(n2r-1), 
                                                   y = pitchers_ref_less$IP, 
                                                   xout = seq((n2-1),0)/(n2-1))$y)
  }
  
  pitchers_full$mapped_IP <- rowMeans(mapped_IP_full)
  pitchers_less$mapped_IP <- rowMeans(mapped_IP_less)
  
  m <- rbind(pitchers_full, pitchers_less)
  data.frame(playerID = m$playerID, yearID = m$yearID, 
             mapped_IP_raw = round(m$mapped_IP))
  
}, mc.cores = ncores))

mapped_pitchers_spud <- merge(career_kAB_spud, mapped_quan_p, 
                           by = c('playerID', 'yearID'))
mapped_pitchers_spud <- mapped_pitchers_spud %>%
```

## Simulation for Major League Baseball Example 2

In this simulation, we compute the probability of the paradox using the results from the Normal distribution example above and illustrate it in the application of Major League Baseball (MLB) since it is widely acknowledged that the batting average follows Normal distribution. 

Specifically, we compute the probability that the top batting average in 2023 is lower than the top batting average in the other season, but the players who have the highest batting average in 2023 are more talented than those who have the highest batting average in the other season. We will use the theoretical results from the Normal distribution example above and the probability of all the seasons from 1871 to 2022 compared with 2023.

```{r cache=TRUE}

batters <- bat_dat
cutoff <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(years, mc.cores = ncores, FUN = function(xx){
  m <- batters %>% filter(yearID == xx) %>% filter(PA >= 75)
  data.frame(thres = median(m$PA), yearID = xx)
}))
batters <- merge(batters, cutoff, by = 'yearID')
batters <- batters %>% select(playerID, yearID, lgID, name, age, lgID, AB, 
                              PA, obs_hits, H, thres, bWAR, pops) %>%
  mutate(comp = ifelse(AB != 0, H / AB, 0), full_time = ifelse(PA >= thres, 'Y', 'N'))
batters_schell <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(years, mc.cores = ncores, FUN = function(xx){
  int<- batters %>% filter(yearID == xx)
  lg_avg <- sum(int$H)/sum(int$AB)
  int %>% mutate(comp = (H + lg_avg * 25)/(AB + 25))
}))

para_dat <- batters_schell %>% filter(full_time == 'Y') %>% group_by(yearID) %>%
  summarise(mu = mean(comp), sd = sd(comp), n = n(), N = round(mean(pops)))

set.seed(13)

simu <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  simu_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, n1j, n2k, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  
  Y1 <- sort(rnorm(n1, mu1, sigma1))
  Y2 <- sort(rnorm(n2, mu2, sigma2))
  
  order_pnorm <- function(q = 0, mean = 0, sd = 1, k = 1, n = 1e4){
    p <- pnorm(q, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    pbinom(k - 1, prob = p, size = n, lower.tail = FALSE)
  }
  
  order_pnorm_vec <- function(q, mean = 0, sd = 1){
    q <- sort(q) 
    n <- length(q)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      order_pnorm(q[j], k = j, n = n, mean = mean, sd = sd)
    }))
  }
  
  u1 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y1, mean = mu1, sd = sigma1)
  u2 <- order_pnorm_vec(Y2, mean = mu2, sd = sigma2)
  
  order_Pareto_vec <- function(u, t = 1, alpha = 1.16, npop = 1e4){
    n <- length(u)
    if(length(npop) == 1) npop <- rep(npop, n)
    unlist(lapply(1:n, function(j){
      qPareto(qbeta(u[j], j + npop[j]-n, n + 1 - j), t = t, alpha = alpha)
    }))
  }
  
  # try it out on the percentiles obtained from order_norm_vec
  X1 <- order_Pareto_vec(u1, npop = N1)
  X2 <- order_Pareto_vec(u2, npop = N2)
  return(c(Y1[n1-n1j], Y2[n2-n2k], X1[n1-n1j], X2[n2-n2k]))
}

  res <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:1000, function(xx){
    simu_paradox(n1 = n1, n2 = n2, N1 = N1, N2 = N2, n1j = n1j, n2k = n2k, 
                 mu1 = mu1, mu2 = mu2, sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)
  }, mc.cores = 7)) 
  res <- as.data.frame(res)
  colnames(res) <- c('Y1', 'Y2', 'X1', 'X2')
  return(nrow(res[res$Y1 < res$Y2 & res$X1 > res$X2,]))
}

prob_paradox <- function(n1, n2, N1, N2, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2){
  x <- c(rep((mu2-mu1)/sigma1, n1), rep(0, (n2-1)))
  mu <- rep(0, (n1+n2-1))
  sigma <- diag((n1+n2-1))
  sigma[1:n1, 1:n1] <- sigma[1:n1, 1:n1] + (sigma2^2/sigma1^2)
  sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), 1:n1] <- 
    sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), 1:n1] + (sigma2/sigma1)
  sigma[1:n1, (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] <- 
    sigma[1:n1, (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] + (sigma2/sigma1)
  sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] <- 
    sigma[(n1+1):(n1+n2-1), (n1+1):(n1+n2-1)] + 1
  
  return(n2*pmvnorm(lower = -Inf, upper = x, mean = mu, sigma = sigma) - 
           (N2/(N1+N2)))
}

para_AVG <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(1:152, mc.cores = ncores, FUN = function(xx){
  # res_test <- replicate(100, simu(n1 = para_dat$n[xx], 
  #                               n2 = para_dat$n[153], 
  #                               N1 = para_dat$N[xx], 
  #                               N2 = para_dat$N[153], 
  #                               n1j = 0, 
  #                               n2k = 0, 
  #                               mu1 = para_dat$mu[xx], 
  #                               mu2 = para_dat$mu[153], 
  #                               sigma1 = para_dat$sd[xx], 
  #                               sigma2 = para_dat$sd[153]))
  
  num_test <- mean(replicate(100, prob_paradox(n1 = para_dat$n[153],
                                          n2 = para_dat$n[xx],
                                          N1 = para_dat$N[153],
                                          N2 = para_dat$N[xx],
                                          mu1 = para_dat$mu[153],
                                          mu2 = para_dat$mu[xx],
                                          sigma1 = para_dat$sd[153],
                                          sigma2 = para_dat$sd[xx])))

  # data.frame(yearID = para_dat$yearID[xx], 
  #            simu_prob = mean(res_test)/1000, 
  #            norm_prob = ifelse(num_test < 0, 0, round(num_test, 4)))
  data.frame(yearID = para_dat$yearID[xx], 
             norm_prob = ifelse(num_test < 0, 0, round(num_test, 4)))
}))

knitr::kable(para_AVG)
```
